claims.text: The nanoparticles are near-equiatomic FeCuCrCoNi high-entropy alloys.
The initial FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles have a solid-solution structure.
Molecular dynamics can be used to investigate the thermal behavior of FeCuCrCoNi HEA nanoparticles during heating.
Free-energy calculations can be used to investigate melting properties in multicomponent alloys.
Umbrella sampling or metadynamics can map the free-energy landscape of thermally induced transformations in FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles.
Controlled-heating simulations of particles approximately 2–10 nm in size can capture nanoscale thermal gradients.
Surface melting and phase separation are possible thermally induced structural reconfigurations in HEA nanoparticles.
Free-energy barriers associated with nucleating structural reconfigurations mediate the thermal response of FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles.
Decreasing nanoparticle size increases the surface-to-volume ratio.
The increased surface-to-volume ratio in smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles enhances the influence of surface energy and thermal fluctuations.
Enhanced surface-energy and thermal-fluctuation effects lower the free-energy barrier for structural transformations during heating.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles have lower free-energy barriers for thermally induced structural transformations than larger nanoparticles.
Lower transformation barriers reduce the thermal stability of smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles will exhibit a lower onset temperature for thermal instability than larger nanoparticles.
Larger FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles simulated under identical thermal conditions provide the baseline for size comparisons.
Classical molecular dynamics is applicable to FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles within the specified nanoscale regime.
Predictions may differ at particle sizes where quantum effects become significant.
The direction of the proposed size effect is supported by analogous studies.
The numerical barrier and onset-temperature differences are uncertain because of model approximations and composition-specific factors.
